clinicalPearls: An inducible urticaria in which deep, often painful or burning swellings develop several hours after sustained pressure to the skin
Typical sites reflect everyday pressure: the feet after prolonged standing or walking, the buttocks after sitting, the hands after carrying bags and the waist under tight belts
The characteristic delay of hours between the pressure stimulus and the swelling distinguishes it from immediate mechanical urticarias such as dermographism
The swelling is deep and dermal, more like angioedema than a superficial weal, and may last a day or more
It frequently coexists with chronic spontaneous urticaria and can be a marker of more troublesome, treatment-resistant disease
A pressure-challenge test, applying a weight over the skin for a set period and reviewing hours later, can reproduce the lesions
Management combines reducing sustained pressure with antihistamines, and omalizumab is a valuable option in resistant disease, while systemic steroids are best avoided for maintenance
reference.pathophysiology: Delayed pressure urticaria is thought to result from sustained mechanical pressure triggering a delayed inflammatory response in the deep dermis and subcutis, with mast cell mediator release and recruitment of inflammatory cells that produce a deep, angioedema-like swelling several hours later. The characteristic latency suggests involvement of a cytokine-driven inflammatory cascade rather than the immediate histamine-only mechanism of superficial urticarias. Its frequent coexistence with chronic spontaneous urticaria implies shared underlying mast cell hyper-reactivity.
additionalDifferentials: Cellulitis or other localised inflammatory swelling
additionalInvestigations: Pressure-challenge testing with a weighted stimulus and delayed review to reproduce swelling
History linking swellings to standing, sitting, carrying loads or tight clothing after a delay
Assessment for coexisting chronic spontaneous urticaria
Inflammatory markers, which may be raised during active disease
Exclusion of angioedema of other mechanism where swellings predominate
Screening tests for chronic urticaria as clinically indicated
redFlags: Swelling of the tongue, lips or airway suggesting angioedema requiring urgent assessment
Systemic symptoms such as fever, arthralgia or malaise accompanying flares
Severe disease markedly limiting standing, walking or work
Poor response to standard therapy, prompting review of the diagnosis and escalation
reference.prognosis: Delayed pressure urticaria tends to be persistent, often for years, and can be disabling because everyday pressures provoke it; it is frequently less responsive to antihistamines than other urticarias, but many patients improve with omalizumab and pressure-reduction measures, and it may eventually remit.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because of the delay between pressure and swelling
Relying on maintenance oral corticosteroids, with their attendant harms, rather than using omalizumab
Overlooking coexisting chronic spontaneous urticaria that requires treatment
Mistaking a localised deep swelling for cellulitis and prescribing antibiotics
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on chronic urticaria
management: Trigger management with pressure-reduction measures: cushioning, padded and broad straps, well-fitting footwear, and avoidance of tight belts and prolonged localised pressure
Second-generation H1-antihistamines as first-line therapy, uptitrated as needed, although the response is often incomplete
Omalizumab (anti-IgE) for antihistamine-resistant disease, which frequently responds well
Adjuncts such as leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) or dapsone, reserving short courses of oral corticosteroids for severe flares and avoiding long-term steroid use
Identify and treat coexisting chronic spontaneous urticaria, which commonly accompanies it and signals more troublesome, treatment-resistant disease
Refer to dermatology or allergy services for refractory or disabling disease
